meta.subtitle: Every segment grew in the June quarter, but the price already discounts consensus growth and the Bear case runs through the fee lines

analystCommentary:
Bank of America's second quarter of 2026 was strong on every line the bank reports. Revenue, net of interest expense, rose {+ 15% +} year over year to $31.6 billion, diluted EPS rose {+ 34% +} to $1.21, and the efficiency ratio improved to 59% on 6.6% of operating leverage. Return on average tangible common shareholders' equity was 17.0%, the CET1 ratio was 11.2% against the 10% minimum management cites, and on July 23, 2026 the Board raised the quarterly dividend to $0.32.

Two notes on the pack. The vendor's statement templates are built for industrial companies, so the financials section says once which rows do not apply to a bank, and the report works from the 10-Q and the earnings release instead. The headline capture returned the bank's research notes on other companies rather than news about the bank, so the report carries no post-quarter news.

We rate the shares HOLD with a target range of $58–$68. The quarter is not in question; the price is. At $59.47 the shares trade at 12.8x NTM earnings, and our Base case, consensus FY27E EPS of $5.26 at that same multiple a year out, lands close to the Street's consensus target of $66.00. That leaves modest upside against a Bear case in which fees and net interest income give back the past year's gains together and EPS returns to the FY25 level of $3.82. The call is close to BUY, and the valuation section shows how close.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Bank of America Corporation is a Delaware bank holding company and financial holding company headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, and it operates its banking activities primarily under the Bank of America, N.A. charter. At June 30, 2026 it had $3.5 trillion in assets and approximately 211,000 employees, with operations across the U.S., its territories and more than 35 countries and/or jurisdictions. It serves more than 69 million consumer and small business clients through approximately 3,500 retail financial centers, approximately 15,000 ATMs and digital banking platforms with approximately 50 million active users, and its GWIM businesses report client balances of approximately $4.9 trillion.

The 10-Q reports four business segments, Consumer Banking, Global Wealth & Investment Management (GWIM), Global Banking and Global Markets, with the remaining operations in All Other. The vendor's FY25 mix, which the segment chart follows, puts Consumer Banking at 37.4% ($43.7B), Global Wealth and Investment Management at 21.3% ($24.9B), Global Banking at 20.6% ($24.1B) and Global Markets at 20.6% ($24.1B). The vendor's geographic split lists a Non-US total of 12.0% beside the regional figures that make it up, so the chart counts non-U.S. revenue twice; the usable figure is the United States at 76.0%.

Revenue in the June quarter split almost evenly between net interest income of $15,997 million and noninterest income of $15,561 million. Half of the bank's revenue therefore depends on the rate and funding cycle and half on fees, much of them tied to markets activity, and the valuation turns on how both hold up together.

thesis.body:
The June quarter improved all three of the bank's earnings lines. Net interest income rose {+ 9% +} to $16.0 billion, which the release attributes to Global Markets activity, higher loan and deposit balances and fixed-rate asset repricing, partially offset by the impact of lower interest rates. Noninterest income rose {+ 22% +} on wealth, investment banking and markets activity, noninterest expense rose a slower 8% to $18.6 billion, and provision for credit losses fell to $1.4 billion from $1.6 billion a year earlier.

The franchise case is sound; the valuation case is thinner. At 12.8x NTM earnings the price already discounts the consensus path from EPS of $4.64 in FY26E to $5.26 in FY27E, and that path assumes fee lines hold near a quarter the CEO called exceptional for the markets-facing businesses. Our probability-weighted value sits above the price, but not by enough to clear the BUY tests against a Bear case in which earnings return to the FY25 level, so we rate the shares HOLD.

catalysts: Operating leverage: management raised its full-year 2026 expectation mid-year; the growth section carries the figures.
Capital return: the Board raised the quarterly dividend 14 percent to $0.32 on July 23, 2026, payable September 25, 2026; the capital-allocation section covers repurchases.
Commercial lending is leading loan growth, and management says investment banking pipelines remain strong and commercial borrowing has picked up.
AI-enabled tools that management says are now embedded across operations and client-facing teams; any benefit would show in the expense line, and the pack does not separate it yet.
risks: Lower rates: the February 2026 10-K says lower interest rates would typically mean lower net interest income; the risk section carries the mechanism.
Fee lines at a high: trading and investment banking led the quarter's growth and, in our view, are the lines most exposed to a market downturn.
Credit: provision and net charge-offs were relatively flat to the March quarter; the risk section covers what would move them.
Litigation and regulation: the 10-Q lists open matters from unemployment-benefit processing to Zelle-related fraud, and capital rules the Board does not control.
Governance: the 2025 Say on Pay vote is the weakest signal in the proxy; the management section carries the detail.

financials.incomeCommentary:
The vendor's income table is gross of interest expense, so it is not a bank's revenue line. Its revenue series runs from $93.9B in FY21 to $191.6B in FY25, and its gross margin (99.8% in FY21, 56.1% in FY25) is not a franchise measure for a bank. The snapshot's Q2'26 revenue of $49.4B (+6%) is on the same gross basis, while the 10-Q and the release report revenue, net of interest expense, of $31.6 billion against $27.4 billion a year earlier; the report uses the bank's net basis throughout. Consensus FY26E revenue of ~$124B carries no basis note. Our reading is that it sits on the net basis, because the six months to June produced $61,830 million of revenue net of interest expense, about half of that estimate; if so, the -35% shown against FY25 is a change of basis rather than a forecast. The vendor's operating income ran from $34.0B in FY21 to a low of $28.3B in FY23 and $37.7B in FY25, and FY25 net income was $30.5B with diluted EPS of $3.82.

On the bank's basis the June quarter reads as follows. Net interest yield on a fully taxable-equivalent basis rose 14 bps to 2.08 percent. Noninterest expense rose 8%, which the release attributes equally to revenue-related expenses and investments in people, brand and technology. Pretax income rose to $11.6 billion from $8.7 billion, net income was $9.1 billion against $7.2 billion, and diluted EPS was $1.21 against $0.90; six-month diluted EPS was $2.31 against $1.79. The efficiency ratio improved 359 bps to 59%, return on average assets was 1.03%, return on average common shareholders' equity was 12.7% and return on average tangible common shareholders' equity was 17.0%, up from 13.6% a year earlier.
financials.balanceCommentary:
The vendor's balance-sheet and leverage rows do not apply to a bank either. FY25 total debt of $365.9B and net debt of $134.1B leave out the deposits that fund most of the balance sheet, and the current ratio, trailing net debt to EBITDA of 15.4x and interest coverage of 0.6x treat deposit funding and interest expense as an industrial company's would, so we draw no conclusion from them. The 10-Q gives the usable frame. Total assets were $3,499,191 million at June 30, 2026, up $87.5 billion from December 31, 2025, primarily on securities borrowed or purchased under agreements to resell and customer receivables supporting Global Markets client activity and on commercial loan growth, partially offset by lower debt securities. Total deposits of $2,025,124 million exceeded total loans and leases of $1,217,619 million, and the release puts average Global Liquidity Sources at $947 billion.

Capital is the binding constraint. CET1 capital was $202 billion, up $1.9 billion from the March quarter, and the CET1 ratio was 11.2% on the standardized approach, which management says is well ahead of its 10% minimum; risk-weighted assets rose to $1.8 trillion on loan growth and capital markets activity. Total shareholders' equity fell $2.1 billion from December 31, 2025 to $301,094 million, which the 10-Q attributes primarily to repurchases, dividends, lower accumulated other comprehensive income and a preferred stock redemption, partially offset by net income. Book value per common share rose 7% to $39.34 and tangible book value per common share rose 7% to $29.37.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash flow is the least informative statement for a bank. The vendor's operating cash flow moves from $45.0B in FY23 to -$8.8B in FY24 and $12.6B in FY25, the table shows capital expenditure of $0.00, and free cash flow therefore repeats operating cash flow. The trailing FCF yield of 22.4% inherits the same problem, and we do not use it.

The capital-return rows do carry information. Share repurchases were $4.6B in FY23, $13.1B in FY24 and $24.1B in FY25, and dividends paid rose each year from $8.1B in FY21 to $9.6B in FY25. Repurchases are the variable part of the payout and dividends the steady part, and the June quarter kept that pattern; the capital-allocation section covers the quarter and the limits on it.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
At $59.47 the shares trade at 13.5x trailing earnings, 12.8x NTM earnings and ~11.3x FY27E EPS of $5.26, with a dividend yield of 1.95%. EV/EBITDA of 24.7x and P/S of 2.2x rest on the vendor's gross revenue and EBITDA and do not apply to a bank, and peer multiples are pending a peer data source, so the page cannot say whether the multiple is cheap or dear against peers. The bank's own anchors are book value per common share of $39.34 and tangible book value per common share of $29.37, earned on a return on average tangible common shareholders' equity of 17.0% in the quarter and 16.52% for the six months.

The Street is constructive: 54 analysts, Buy 35, Hold 18, Sell 1, with a consensus target of $66.00 (+11.0%), a median of $65.00 and a range of $59.00–$75.00. The shares sit in the upper part of their 52-week range of $46.12–$65.23.

Each scenario applies a multiple to the EPS it expects for the year ahead, so the like-for-like reference is today's NTM multiple, not the lower multiple the price implies on FY27E. The Base holds the NTM multiple a year out on FY27E EPS. For holding it: return on tangible equity has risen, operating leverage is running above guidance, and consensus still has EPS growing into FY27E. Against it: the FY27E figure builds on fee lines from a quarter the CEO called exceptional, and a market that comes to see 2026 as a peak in fees would pay less than today's multiple for the next year's earnings. We think the two arguments balance, and the Base multiple decides the label more than any other input.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Operating leverage lands at or above the top of the 300-400 basis point range guided for 2026 and stays positive into 2027, fees hold near the June-quarter level and credit costs stay near the $1.4 billion quarterly run-rate, so FY27E consensus EPS is met. The market pays 14x for it: our assumption, a step above the 13.5x trailing multiple for return on tangible equity held near 17.0%. That is $73.64, just below the Street's high target of $75.00.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus is met: EPS of $4.64 in FY26E and $5.26 in FY27E. Credit stays near the current run-rate, the CET1 ratio stays near 11.2% with repurchases absorbing the excess, and the shares hold today's 12.8x NTM multiple a year out, applied to FY27E EPS. That is $67.33, close to the Street's consensus target of $66.00.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Rate cuts compress net interest income faster than repricing offsets them, trading and investment banking fall back toward year-ago levels, and provision rises as credit normalizes, so EPS returns to the FY25 level of $3.82. A market pricing falling earnings pays less than the Base's NTM multiple; we assume 12x, a small discount because capital and deposits stay intact. That is $45.84, just under the 52-week low of $46.12.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight the Base at 55%, the Bull at 25% and the Bear at 20%. The weighted fair value is $64.61, an expected upside of +8.6%, against a bear-case downside of -22.9% and a reward/risk of 0.38×. That derives HOLD: expected upside is short of the +10.0%, and reward/risk short of the 0.50×, that the BUY label needs.

Each weight rests on its own evidence. The Base gets most of the weight because six-month diluted EPS of $2.31 is already about half the FY26E consensus, so the near-term path is largely in hand. The Bull gets a quarter because first-half operating leverage ran above the raised guidance and every segment grew, but it also needs a multiple above the trailing one on fees the CEO called exceptional. The Bear gets less than the Bull because it needs all three earnings lines to turn at once, and the current credit evidence runs the other way: net charge-offs were relatively flat to the March quarter and reservable criticized commercial exposures fell. It is not smaller, because the 10-K's rate mechanism and the fee cycle are both live.

The call is close to BUY. Holding the Bear at today's NTM multiple instead of our discounted one lifts expected upside to just under the BUY threshold; a Base at the trailing multiple on FY27E derives a narrow BUY; and moving a third of the Bear weight to the Bull case does the same. Moving a quarter of it lifts expected upside past the threshold but leaves reward/risk under its bar, which is the test that binds. In the other direction, a Base at 12x FY27E, our assumption for a modest de-rating, or swapping the Bull and Bear weights, still derives HOLD, and even a Bear weighted well above the Bull on top of that lower Base stays HOLD. We think the NTM multiple on FY27E is the honest Base and that the Bear multiple belongs below it, so HOLD is the call.

segments.name: Consumer Banking Segment
segments.body: Consumer Banking is the deposit engine. June-quarter revenue was $11,336 million, up 5%, driven primarily by higher net interest income, and net income was $3,281 million; provision fell to $1.2 billion with a net reserve release of $23 million against a net reserve build of $82 million a year earlier. The efficiency ratio was 51% and the return on average allocated capital 29%. Average deposits of $957 billion are up from pre-pandemic levels per the release, 59% of deposits sit in checking accounts, and the release ranks the bank first in U.S. consumer deposits on first-quarter 2026 FFIEC call-report data. The card book cuts the other way: the risk-adjusted margin slipped to 6.5% from 7.1% a year earlier while average balances grew to $103.6 billion.

segments.name: Global Wealth and Investment Management Segment
segments.body: GWIM showed the clearest margin gain in the quarter. Revenue rose 16% to $6,871 million on asset management fees up 19% to $4.4 billion, which the release attributes to higher market valuations and solid AUM flows, as well as higher NII; net income rose to $1,413 million from $993 million, and the pretax margin reached 27% from 22% a year earlier. Client balances were $4.9 trillion, up 12% driven primarily by market valuations, and assets under management $2.3 trillion, up 17%, with AUM flows of $13.7 billion in the quarter and $78 billion since the second quarter of 2025. Average loans and leases rose 14% to $270 billion. Fee revenue here moves with markets, and a quarter's flows are small beside the balances they are added to.

segments.name: Global Banking Segment
segments.body: Global Banking is the corporate lending, treasury and investment banking franchise. Per the call, revenue rose 10% to $6.2 billion and net income 20% to more than $2 billion, with total corporate investment banking fees, excluding self-led deals, up 50% to more than $2.1 billion across debt underwriting, advisory and equity underwriting. Average deposits rose 8% to $652 billion and average loans 7% to $413 billion, the release cites higher treasury service charges, and the return on allocated capital was 15%. The pack shows the fee growth but not whether it reflects share gains or a strong market, so we read it as mostly market conditions.

segments.name: Global Markets Segment
segments.body: Global Markets produced the quarter's sharpest growth. Sales and trading revenue was $7.1 billion including net DVA losses of $57 million, up 33% including and excluding net DVA, with equities up 70% to $3.6 billion on client financing activity and trading in derivatives and cash, and FICC up 9% to $3.5 billion; segment net income was $2.6 billion, and $2.7 billion excluding DVA per the call. The release counts 17 consecutive quarters of year-over-year sales and trading growth, and the call adds 14 consecutive quarters of year-over-year net income growth, which shows a franchise that has grown through several market conditions; whether it gained share the pack cannot say. This is also the segment most directly exposed to the market downturn the February 2026 10-K lists first among its risk factors.

moatFactors.name: Deposit franchise
moatFactors.body: Average deposits of $2.02 trillion grew for a 12th consecutive quarter of sequential average growth per the release, and the call puts the rate paid on consumer deposits at 48 basis points. Low-cost, growing deposits fund the loan book with room to spare and are the base of net interest income. The pressure point is the net interest yield of 2.08 percent: if deposit costs rise faster than asset yields reprice, that yield is where it shows.

moatFactors.name: Scale and digital distribution
moatFactors.body: The branch, ATM and digital footprint in the company overview reaches more than 69 million clients, and the release reports that most Consumer Banking sales were digitally enabled, with 4.4 billion digital logins and 24.6 million active Erica users in the quarter. In our view that scale is what lets every segment add operating leverage while still investing, and it shows in the efficiency ratio. Scale also concentrates operational and regulatory exposure, which the 10-Q's list of open matters illustrates.

moatFactors.name: Integrated model
moatFactors.body: Consumer Banking, GWIM and Global Banking feed each other: 38.7 million consumer checking accounts, 92% of them primary; $640 billion of consumer investment assets, up 18% with $19 billion of net client flows; and ~6K net new $500K+ relationships across Merrill and the Private Bank in the quarter per the release. Integration cuts both ways: the wealth and markets businesses are the ones most sensitive to asset prices, so the model raises the sensitivity of earnings to markets as well as the stickiness of clients.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat wide because its base, low-cost and growing deposits funding a loan book with room to spare, is in place, and because each of the four segments grew revenue and net income on its own account in the quarter. Three things could erode it: a rate path that lifts deposit costs while asset yields fall, a credit cycle that raises losses above the current run-rate, and a reset of capital rules that limits how much the bank can grow and return. The consecutive-quarter streaks the release and the call count in deposits, loans and trading show a franchise that has compounded through several conditions; they do not show that the June quarter's fee revenue will repeat, and we keep those two points apart.

points: Management now expects full-year 2026 operating leverage of 300-400 basis points, after first-half operating leverage exceeded 450 basis points, up from the more than 200 basis points it guided in April. The sustainable aim it described at Investor Day sits below that range, so 2026 is running above the aim and 2027 starts from a high base.

Net interest income for the six months was $31,742 million against $29,113 million a year earlier, and the call adds the repayment of higher-cost funding to the repricing the release cites. Whether that growth continues depends on repricing outrunning lower rates, which the risk section weighs.

Average loans and leases of $1.22 trillion rose 8% from a year ago, with growth in every business segment and a ninth consecutive quarter of sequential average growth; average commercial loans rose 11% to $733 billion. Growth led by commercial lending is also where the risk section looks for the next credit losses.

Fee lines are growing faster than the balance sheet: the call cites 18% growth in investment brokerage fees, and asset management fees rose 19% to $4.4 billion. Part of that growth is market valuations rather than the franchise, as the release says for wealth, and the moat section carries investment banking and trading.
Consensus has EPS of $4.64 in FY26E and $5.26 in FY27E, and revenue of $124B and $130.5B on the basis the financials section explains.

Client growth underneath: 160K+ net new consumer checking accounts and 30 consecutive quarters of net growth, ~2 million BofA Rewards enrollments since the late-May relaunch, and approximately 6,000 net new affluent households in wealth per the call; these feed next year's deposits and fees.

management.leadership: Brian T. Moynihan is Chair and CEO, as the July 14, 2026 release styles him, and the March 2026 proxy names Mr. Nowell as Lead Independent Director. The proxy reports that the Board determined every director and nominee other than Mr. Moynihan to be independent under the NYSE listing standards and its own Categorical Standards. Alastair M. Borthwick is Executive Vice President and CFO per the release. On execution the record is the quarter: per the call, every segment grew revenue and net income, generated operating leverage and improved its efficiency ratio, and the full-year operating-leverage expectation was raised mid-year. Our reservation is about emphasis rather than conduct: the call and release lean on consecutive-quarter streaks and rankings, which say more about the last several quarters than the next one.
management.capitalAllocation: The bank returned $8.0 billion in the June quarter, $2.0 billion in common dividends and $6.0 billion in repurchases, against net income of $9.1 billion, so repurchases carry most of the payout and the 1.95% dividend yield understates it. The quarterly dividend goes to $0.32 from the $0.28 paid in the quarter, an increase of 14 percent. The limit is regulatory capital: returning most of earnings holds the CET1 ratio steady only while risk-weighted assets grow moderately, and the 10-Q lists stress capital buffer requirements, total loss-absorbing capacity requirements and the GSIB surcharge among uncertainties outside the bank's control. Our judgment is that the allocation is disciplined and the dividend increase affordable; the risk is a rule change that lowers the ceiling, not a management choice.
management.governance: The March 2026 proxy is the source. Say on Pay drew 73.6% of approximately 5.6 billion votes cast at the 2025 annual meeting. During 2025 the company reached out to 74 institutional shareholders representing approximately 67% of institutionally held shares and held 52 meetings with 31 of them. The proxy says that engagement and its assessment of the vote informed the decision to keep the executive compensation design generally consistent; it attributes the tighter performance standard for a 100% payout on the performance restricted stock units granted in February 2026, and the new opportunity to earn up to 150% maximum payout, to the focus on long-term Responsible Growth discussed with investors at the 2025 Investor Day. In our reading a vote below three-quarters is the weakest signal in the proxy, mitigated by an otherwise independent board and a Lead Independent Director. Ordinary-course relationships were tested at less than 2% of gross revenues where applicable, and the related-person policy sends transactions expected to exceed $120,000 to the Corporate Governance Committee. The excerpt does not carry the pay tables, so we make no claim about pay levels.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy's ownership table, as of March 13, 2026, shows that each director and named executive officer, and all directors and executive officers as a group of 25 persons, beneficially owned less than 1% of the common stock. Mr. Moynihan beneficially owned 2,803,195 shares, with a further 1,724,434 stock units, for 4,527,629 in total, and the group held 18,963,591 shares and units combined. Three holders were above 5% at that date: The Vanguard Group at 9.1%, Warren E. Buffett/Berkshire Hathaway Inc. at 7.9% and BlackRock, Inc. at 6.9%. Insider holdings are meaningful to the executives personally but immaterial to control, and the pack carries no insider transaction data.

idiosyncratic: Rate cycle and net interest income. The February 2026 10-K says a change in monetary policy resulting in lower interest rates would typically result in lower revenue through lower net interest income, and notes that the Federal Reserve reduced policy rates in 2025 with uncertainty over the pace and duration of further reductions. The June-quarter release already shows the effect, with NII growth partially offset by the impact of lower interest rates. Net interest income is the larger of the two revenue lines, so the pace of cuts against the pace of repricing is the Bear case's first mechanism.

Fees at the top of the cycle. The trading and investment-banking growth the Global Markets and Global Banking segments show led the quarter, and the 10-K says a market downturn could reduce noninterest income as well as net interest income. A return to year-ago levels in those lines would remove much of the quarter's revenue growth, and the equities line, whose growth outpaced FICC's, is the one we would watch first.

Credit normalization. Provision and net charge-offs of $1.4 billion each were relatively flat to the March quarter and below a year earlier; reservable criticized commercial exposures fell approximately $2.3 billion to roughly $22 billion, and non-performing loans were stable at approximately $5.8 billion. The risk is the one the 10-Q names, future credit losses higher than expected if unemployment, real estate prices or corporate bond spreads move. The card book's falling risk-adjusted margin is the early signal to watch, and a modest reserve release in a quarter of loan growth leaves less built ahead of a turn.

Litigation, regulation and operational exposure. The 10-Q's forward-looking statement lists open matters, including unemployment-benefit processing for California and certain other states, the automatic credit card payment service, anti-money-laundering and economic sanctions programs, and Zelle-related fraud, along with potential changes to loss allocations between financial institutions and customers. None is quantified in the pack, and the bank's own statement that future liabilities may be in excess of its recorded liability and estimated range of possible loss is the risk in its own words.
risks.systemic: The systemic exposures are those of a global systemically important bank. The February 2026 10-K's market risk factor runs from interest rates, inflation and Federal Reserve policy through fiscal and debt-ceiling risk, tariffs, geopolitical events, bank and nonbank failures and the volatility of digital assets; the 10-Q's forward-looking statement adds sovereign debt stress outside the U.S. and a deterioration in private credit markets. The backdrop the call describes is benign: the bank's research team raised its 2026 U.S. GDP growth forecast to 2.2%, expects global growth of 3.2% in 2026 and 3.5% in 2027, and consumer spending was running at 6% plus year over year. The point to hold onto is that a downturn hits all three earnings lines at once, net interest income through rates, fees through markets and provision through credit, which is why the Bear case moves EPS and the multiple together.

body: **HOLD, target range $58–$68.** The June quarter showed every segment growing revenue and net income with operating leverage. At 12.8x NTM earnings, though, the price already discounts consensus EPS growth into FY27E, and our weighted value of $64.61 leaves expected upside of +8.6% against a Bear case near the 52-week low, short of both BUY tests.

What we value is the deposit and lending franchise and the capital it generates. What keeps us from a BUY at this price is that the past year's gains in fees and net interest income are the ones a rate and market cycle can reverse together. We read the shares as fairly priced for the consensus path, a step below the Street's consensus Buy.

On unchanged scenarios, a fall in the price to the bottom of our range would derive BUY, and a rise to just above the top of it would derive SELL. On the evidence, a second half that confirms the raised operating-leverage expectation with credit costs near the current run-rate would support the trailing 13.5x multiple on FY27E in the Base, which derives BUY; a year-over-year decline in sales and trading or in net interest income would raise the Bear weight.
